title: What helps and hinders communication
blurb: Use the sender-receiver model to explain noise, and name the factors that help or hinder project communication.
question: A UK project manager emails an urgent design change, full of acronyms, to an engineering team eight time zones away at the end of the UK day. The team builds to the old design. Using the sender-receiver model, what went wrong, and which factors would have improved the outcome?

teach.h: Meaning sent is not always meaning received
teach.body: Communication succeeds when the meaning the receiver takes is the meaning the sender intended. The widely used sender-receiver model breaks this down: a sender encodes an idea into a message, sends it through a channel, and the receiver decodes it. Feedback from the receiver shows whether it landed. Noise is anything that distorts or blocks the message at any stage. In plain English: what you said is not always what they heard.

teach.caption: Noise can strike at any step: poor encoding, a faulty channel, or decoding coloured by assumptions.
A helpful way to group the negative factors. Noise is not just sound: it is anything that gets in the way of meaning.

teach.h: Positive factors and the barriers they beat

teach.body: A one-way message can't tell you whether noise has crept in. Feedback can. Active listening means giving full attention, asking questions, and paraphrasing back what you heard so misunderstandings surface immediately. Trust matters too: people who feel safe will admit they're confused or challenge a senior colleague. Choosing the right channel and timing reduces noise before it starts, which is why sensitive or complex messages suit interactive methods.

teach.h: Scenario: Kestrel Engineering's offshore design team
teach.body: The UK project manager emails 'Switch FAT spec to Rev C ASAP' at 6pm, late evening for the team in India. The acronyms mean different things to different readers, the email sits unread overnight among dozens of others, and a junior engineer who is unsure doesn't question a senior manager. Noise at every stage. The fix: a short call in overlapping hours, plain words, a confirm-back of what will change, and an open invitation to ask questions.

teach.h: Barrier and what the project manager can do
head: Barrier
Practical response
rows: Test tools, agree a backup channel
Target and prioritise; flag key items
Pick timing; face to face; empathy
Invite challenge; make it safe to ask
One agreed source of key messages

teach.h: Where noise creeps in by life cycle

teach.text: Exam traps: 'noise' means ANY interference, not just sound; feedback travels from receiver back to sender; and the receiver, not the sender, does the decoding. Also, more messages don't overcome barriers: information overload is itself a barrier.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Name the factor precisely, e.g. 'jargon' or 'status and hierarchy', not just 'poor communication'.
Say whether it helps or hinders, and where it acts in the sender-receiver model.
Explain its effect on the project: misunderstanding, rework, delay, lost support.
Give a practical response the project manager would take.
Use a different factor for each mark; don't repeat one idea in new words.
Model: sender, encode, channel, decode, receiver, with feedback closing the loop.
Noise is anything that distorts or blocks meaning, at any stage.
Helps: clarity, trust, active listening, feedback, right channel and timing, shared language.
Hinders: jargon, language and culture, distance, technology, overload, emotions, assumptions, status, poor timing, conflicting messages.
Each barrier has a practical fix; feedback is how you find out noise got in.

summary: You can now explain the sender-receiver model, what noise is and where it occurs. You can also name the factors that help and hinder project communication and suggest a practical response to each barrier.

A.q: In the sender-receiver model of communication, what is 'noise'?
options: Only background sound in a meeting room
The receiver's reply sent back to the sender
The channel chosen to carry the message
Anything that distorts or blocks a message
A.why: Noise is any interference, physical, technical, language-based or personal, that distorts or blocks the intended meaning.

whyNot.0: Background sound is one form of noise, but the term covers far more than sound.
whyNot.2: The channel is the medium; noise is what interferes with it or with understanding.

A.q: In the sender-receiver model, what is the purpose of FEEDBACK?
options: To confirm the message was understood
To encode the message into words
To choose the most suitable channel to use
To add more detail for the receiver
A.why: Feedback from the receiver tells the sender whether the meaning was received as intended, so errors can be corrected.

whyNot.1: Encoding is done by the sender before the message is sent.
whyNot.2: Choosing a channel is the sender's decision, made before sending.
whyNot.3: Adding detail is part of encoding, not the purpose of feedback.

A.q: Which of the following is a factor that POSITIVELY affects communication?
A.why: Active listening (attention, questions, paraphrasing back) helps the receiver understand and surfaces misunderstandings early.

whyNot.0: Information overload buries key messages, so it is a barrier.
whyNot.1: Status and hierarchy can stop people asking questions or challenging, so it is a barrier.
whyNot.3: Conflicting messages confuse receivers, so they are a barrier.

B.q: A project manager's update to retail store staff is full of IT acronyms that staff don't recognise. Which barrier is this?
B.why: Specialist terms the audience doesn't share are jargon, which stops the receiver decoding the message.

whyNot.0: Overload is about too much information, not unfamiliar terms.
whyNot.2: Nothing in the scenario says the timing was wrong.
whyNot.3: Distance isn't the problem; the words themselves are.

B.q: At which stage of the sender-receiver model does the RECEIVER's own interpretation of the message happen?
B.why: Decoding is where the receiver interprets the message, shaped by their knowledge, language, assumptions and feelings.

whyNot.0: Encoding is the sender turning an idea into a message.
whyNot.1: Transmission is the message travelling through the channel.
whyNot.2: Feedback is the receiver's response back to the sender, after decoding.

B.q: A junior engineer spots an error in a senior designer's drawing but says nothing. Which barrier is most likely at work?
B.why: A perceived gap in seniority can make people reluctant to question or challenge, so problems go unreported.

whyNot.1: Overload would mean the engineer missed information; here they noticed but didn't speak.
whyNot.3: Nothing suggests the two are apart; the barrier is about seniority.

C.q:
Which THREE are negative factors (barriers) to communication?
1. Assumptions
2. Shared language
3. Emotions
4. Conflicting messages
C.why: Assumptions, emotions and conflicting messages all distort meaning. A shared language helps communication.

whyNot.0: Shared language is a positive factor, and conflicting messages are missing.
whyNot.1: Shared language is a positive factor, and emotions are missing.
whyNot.3: Shared language is a positive factor, and assumptions are missing.

C.q: Two members of a project board send a supplier different instructions about the same change. What is the best way to remove this barrier?
options: Ask the supplier to choose one
Agree one source of key messages
Send all instructions by formal letter
C.why: Conflicting messages are removed by agreeing a single, authoritative source and sender for key instructions.

whyNot.0: Leaving the supplier to choose shifts the problem and risks the wrong work being done.
whyNot.2: More emails add overload and may add further conflicting versions.
whyNot.3: Changing the channel doesn't stop two people sending different content.

C.q: A UK project manager always holds the weekly team call at a time that falls late at night for colleagues in Sydney, who often miss it or seem disengaged. What is the best response?
options: Send the slides to the UK team only
Replace the call with longer emails
Rotate times and record each call
C.why: Rotating times shares the inconvenience fairly and recording gives access to anyone who can't attend, tackling the time-zone barrier.

whyNot.0: Forcing late-night attendance ignores the barrier and harms wellbeing and engagement.
whyNot.1: Leaving the Sydney team out makes the communication gap worse.
whyNot.2: Longer emails lose the interactive element and may add overload.

reteach.title: Ordering a takeaway from a noisy party
reteach.question: You phone in a takeaway order from a loud party with poor signal, and the wrong food arrives. Where in the sender-receiver model did it go wrong?

blocks.h: Every stage of the model at work
blocks.body: You are the sender. You encode your order as 'two of the usual and a 42', jargon only you understand. The channel is a crackly phone line, and the music behind you is noise. The person taking the order decodes '42' as '24' and guesses what 'the usual' means. Nobody reads the order back, so there's no feedback to catch the mistake. Wrong curry, every stage contributing.

steps.label: Encode
steps.sub: Say the dish names, not 'the usual'

steps.label: Channel
steps.sub: Step outside or order through the app

steps.label: Decode
steps.sub: Speak clearly, spell out anything unusual

steps.label: Feedback
steps.sub: Ask them to read the order back

blocks.text: Shouting the order louder (more of the same message) doesn't fix it. Clear encoding, a better channel and feedback do. On a project, more emails don't beat noise either.

explain.body: The sender has an idea and encodes it into words, visuals and tone. The message travels through a channel. The receiver decodes it, interpreting it through their own knowledge and experience. Feedback goes back to the sender to confirm or correct understanding.

test.q: Choosing the words, images and tone used to express an idea is which stage of the model?
test.why: Encoding is the sender turning an idea into a message: the choice of words, visuals and tone.

whyNot.0: Decoding is the receiver interpreting the message.
whyNot.1: Feedback is the receiver's response to the sender.
whyNot.3: The channel is the medium the message travels through.

explain.body: Noise is anything that distorts or blocks a message. It can be in the channel (a frozen video call), in the encoding (jargon, unclear wording) or in the decoding (assumptions, emotions, cultural differences). Because it can occur anywhere, feedback is needed to detect it.

test.q: A video call keeps freezing during a design review, so key points are missed. In model terms, this is best described as…
test.why: A technology failure interfering with transmission is noise in the channel.

whyNot.1: The sender's wording isn't the problem; the call itself is failing.
whyNot.2: Feedback is a response from the receiver, not a fault.
whyNot.3: Decoding is interpretation; here the message never arrives intact.

explain.body: Positive factors: clarity, trust, active listening, feedback, the right channel and timing, and a shared language. Active listening means full attention, questions and paraphrasing back. Trust lets people admit confusion or challenge seniors.

test.q: Which practice best demonstrates active listening?
options: Preparing your reply while they talk
test.why: Paraphrasing back shows attention and lets the speaker confirm or correct your understanding.

whyNot.0: Planning your reply means you're not fully listening.
whyNot.1: A summary is useful for the record, but it isn't active listening in the conversation.
whyNot.2: Questions are a core part of active listening.

explain.body: Barriers: jargon, language and cultural differences, distance and time zones, technology problems, information overload, emotions, assumptions, status and hierarchy, poor timing and conflicting messages. Each has a practical response, from plain language and overlap hours to prioritising key messages and making it safe to challenge.

test.q: Stakeholders receive so many project updates that they miss an important safety notice. Which action best removes this barrier?
options: Send the notice again by email
Add the notice to the weekly newsletter
test.why: The barrier is information overload, so the fix is fewer, targeted messages with critical items clearly flagged.

whyNot.0: Another email adds to the overload that caused the problem.
whyNot.2: Burying it in a newsletter makes it easier to miss.
whyNot.3: A longer meeting adds volume rather than focusing attention.
